hints: Think about why an M+1 peak appears at all, which isotope of carbon is responsible and what its natural abundance of about 1.1% means for each carbon present.
walkthrough:
Link M+1 to carbon-13**
You are sitting with a mass spectrum where M is all $^{12}\text{C}$ and M+1 is the same ion but with one $^{13}\text{C}$ in place of $^{12}\text{C}$. Each carbon atom in the molecule has about a 1.1% chance of being $^{13}\text{C}$, so the bigger the molecule in carbons, the bigger the M+1 peak relative to M.

Apply the standard relationship**
The trusted formula is: $$n(\text{C}) = \frac{100 \times \text{height of M+1}}{\text{height of M} \times 1.1}$$ Put in your numbers: $$n = \frac{100 \times 1.25}{22.65 \times 1.1} = 5.02$$ That rounds cleanly to 5, confirming $\text{C}_5$ in $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_2$.
Final answer: no. of C atoms $= \dfrac{100 \times 1.25}{22.65 \times 1.1} = 5.02 \approx 5$, so one molecule of X contains five carbon atoms.

hints: Calculate the $M_r$ of $[\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_2]^+$ and subtract 57 to find the mass lost as the neutral fragment.
Use the molecular formula to split $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_2$ into two parts, one with mass 57 that carries the positive charge and is seen, and one neutral part that is not seen.
walkthrough:
Work out what must add up**
The molecular ion is $M_r = (5 \times 12) + 10 + 32 = 102$. If the detector sees a cation at $m/e = 57$, the rest of the mass must be $102 - 57 = 45$ and must leave as an uncharged radical or molecule.

Assign the two formulae**
Try $\text{C}_3\text{H}_5\text{O}$: $(3 \times 12)+5+16 = 57$. That fits the observed peak perfectly, and it must carry the $+$ charge because only ions are detected. The remainder is $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{O}$: $(2 \times 12)+5+16 = 45$. So write: $$[\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_2]^+ \rightarrow [\text{C}_3\text{H}_5\text{O}]^+ + \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{O}$$

hints: Recall that proton NMR needs a zero point for chemical shift and a liquid that dissolves the sample but has no $^1\text{H}$ to interfere.
walkthrough:
Give each chemical its job**
Think of TMS, $\text{Si}(\text{CH}_3)_4$, as the anchor. It gives one sharp singlet well away from most signals and is defined as $\delta = 0$. $\text{CDCl}_3$ is deuterochloroform. It is a good solvent for organic samples, it has D not H so it gives no proton signal, and it is inert.

Final answer: TMS: reference standard for 0 ppm chemical shift.
$\text{CDCl}_3$: inert solvent that dissolves sample but contains no protons.

hints: Match the numbers on the spectrum (3, 3+2, 2) to proton counts and note the singlet, triplet and quartet splitting patterns.
Use the Data Booklet ranges: protons next to $\text{C=O}$ appear around $\delta$ 2.0 to 2.5, protons on carbon attached to oxygen appear around $\delta$ 3.3 to 4.3.
Pair the triplet at $\delta$ 1.2 with the quartet at $\delta$ 3.5 as a classic $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2$ group split by each other, and check what deshields the $\text{CH}_2$ so strongly.
walkthrough:
Read the singlet at 2.2 ppm**
You see area 3, a singlet, at $\delta$ 2.2. Three protons with no neighbours means a $\text{CH}_3$ next to something with no H, and $\delta$ 2.2 is classic for $\text{CH}_3$ next to $\text{C=O}$. So this is $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}$, an acetyl type fragment.

Pair the 1.2 and 3.5 ppm signals**
You see area 3 triplet at $\delta$ 1.2 and area 2 quartet at $\delta$ 3.5. That triplet plus quartet pair is the fingerprint of $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2$. The $\text{CH}_2$ is strongly deshielded to 3.5, which tells you it is directly attached to electronegative oxygen. So this is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{O}$.

Assign the singlet at 4.0 ppm**
You see area 2, a singlet, at $\delta$ 4.0. Two protons with no neighbours, very deshielded, so the $\text{CH}_2$ must be attached to two electron withdrawing groups. Putting the pieces together, it sits between $\text{C=O}$ and O: $(\text{CO})\text{CH}_2\text{O}$. Total H is $3+3+2+2 = 10$, matching $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_2$.

Final answer: peak at $\delta$ 2.2 (singlet, 3H): $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}$
peaks at $\delta$ 1.2 (triplet, 3H) and $\delta$ 3.5 (quartet, 2H): $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{O}$
peak at $\delta$ 4.0 (singlet, 2H): $(\text{CO})\text{CH}_2\text{O}$

hints: Remember that a yellow precipitate with alkaline aqueous iodine identifies $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}$ or $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)}$, then join the three fragments from (c)(i) in the only order that keeps that group intact.
walkthrough:
Join the fragments with the positive test**
The yellow precipitate is $\text{CHI}_3$ from the triiodomethane test, proving a methyl ketone $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}$. You already have $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}$, $\text{CH}_2$ between C=O and O, and $\text{OCH}_2\text{CH}_3$. Linking them gives only one sensible chain: $$\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_2\text{OCH}_2\text{CH}_3$$ This is 1-ethoxypropan-2-one.

hints: Think about what group gives 9 equivalent protons as a single peak, and what single proton ester fragment is left to make $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_2$.
walkthrough:
Spot the 9 to 1 clue**
Only two peaks in ratio 9:1 means 9H in one identical environment and 1H in another. Nine equivalent H screams $\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_3$, three identical methyl groups on one carbon with no neighbouring H, so a big singlet. As an ester $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_2$, the 1H must be the formate H in $\text{HCOO}$. Join them: $$\text{HCO}_2\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_3$$ tert-butyl methanoate.

hints: Focus on the carbon atom itself, how many groups it holds and how they must differ to make mirror images non-superimposable.
walkthrough:
State the textbook test for chirality**
Picture a carbon with four single bonds. If all four attached atoms or groups are different, the carbon is a stereocentre. Its mirror image cannot be superimposed, so the molecule can show optical isomerism.
Final answer: a carbon atom with four different atoms or groups attached to it

hints: Draw a $\text{C}_5$ carboxylic acid skeleton $\text{COOH}$ plus four carbons, then place a methyl branch so that one carbon carries four different groups.
walkthrough:
Build a branched acid**
A straight chain acid $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$ has no chiral carbon. Move one methyl as a branch onto C2: $$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{COOH}$$ Now C2 is attached to H, $\text{CH}_3$, $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{COOH}$, four different groups, so it is chiral. This is 2-methylbutanoic acid.
